https://www.dw.com/en/munich-prosecutors.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J7uF The 1970 arson attack on a Jewish religious center in central Munich killed seven people [FILE: February 13, 1970] Image: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Munich 's Public Prosecutor's Office believes it has solved one of the worst antisemitic attacks in post-war German history. Police and prosecutors said on Thursday that new investigations point "clearly" towards the involvement of a man who died in 2020. Additional information came to light after his death which led to the case being reopened in April 2025. Now, with investigators satisfied that the culprit is identified — but with no scope to prosecute the deceased and no known indications of accomplices — they are closing the file once again. West Germany's president at the time, Gustav Heinemann, attended the memorial ceremony in Munich Image: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance What is the case about? On February 13, 1970, a fire broke out at the Jewish religious community for Munich and Upper Bavaria , in the area incorporating its retirement home, killing seven people. All of them had survived the Holocaust and two were inmates in Nazi German concentration camps. Prosecutors said the fire was set using a "gasoline mixture" that was sprinkled and lit in several different places in a stairwell, hoping to ensure that it spread. Another 15 people were wounded in the fire, four of them seriously. The building in central Munich sustained severe damages, particularly on the upper levels as a result of the stack effect channeling the flames up the stairwell. The attack took place three days after an attack at Munich-Riem airport by Palestinian terrorists; the victim from that attack was mourned along with the seven killed in the fire Image: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance What led investigators to reopen the file? Investigations were originally halted in 2017, almost 50 years after the suspected homicides. Prosecutors and Munich's police precinct explained what led them to reopening the case in Thursday's joint statement. "A witness provided credible information on the suspect," they said. "She said that the suspect had been in close contact with one of her close relatives in the 1970s. Shortly after the death of this relative, she revealed her knowledge on the matter." Authorities reviewed old files and also interviewed contacts of the suspect in the renewed investigation. The fire caused considerable damage on the upper levels; a reward was offered at the time but the culprit was never caught Image: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance What did investigators say about the suspect? Prosecutors did not identify the suspect, and stressed that posthumous prosecution was not possible in Germany and that the presumption of innocence still applied in death. They identified him as a man who died in 2020 and who was 25 years old at the time of the attack. He was regularly in the area of the religious center on Reichenbachstrasse at the time, they said. On the evening of the fire, investigators said he was alleged to have complained that "the Jews have everything" while standing in sight of the old people's home and to have expressed a desire to set them alight. Within a quarter of an hour, the building was ablaze, prosecutors said. "These allegations are based on credible statements from the witness, who in turn was relaying what her deceased relative told her," the prosecutor's office said. "Additional relatives confirmed these statements." What did prior background investigations reveal? Prosecutors also said that background investigations further solidified their suspicions. The suspect was a known member of the far-right community in Munich at the time, with witnesses describing him as an antisemite with a "Hitler obsession." In his youth he had listened to Hitler speeches on records. He practiced shooting near Adolf Hitler 's Berghof holiday home in the Bavarian Alps, the site of multiple antisemitic crimes against humanity in the Nazi era. He had a history of using explosives and a juvenile conviction for blowing up two telephone booths in the 1960s. A headteacher also recalled a violent incident from his youth when he pulled a Hitler youth dagger which he said was a gift from his father. Prosecutors said it was not possible to say whether the suspect acted alone or in a group with certainty, but also said the investigations had not found any indications of accomplices. "All in all, the new investigations conducted after the reopening of the case speak clearly for the suspect's involvement," prosecutors concluded, albeit with it no longer being possible to try the case in a court of law. https://www.foxnews.com/world/finlands-s.text: UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war. "I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others." Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments. KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE "I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said. The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow. Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT "That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus," Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin, unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response. Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer. "Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said. But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia. "As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe. Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. "We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads." His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it." Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor. "We are calm because we are prepared," he said. He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed. That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government. The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release. "We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6." FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT "We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia." He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO." Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter." Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers, including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities. Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis. WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR? Asked about Trump’s call at the U.N. for countries to support efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, Stubb was unequivocal. "I agree, Iran should not obtain nuclear weapons," he told Fox News Digital, adding that Tehran should not use proxies or be able to produce missiles. Stubb also argued that the conflicts involving Russia and Iran can no longer be viewed in isolation, alleging that Moscow is providing intelligence to Tehran that Iran has used against U.S. military bases in the Gulf, while Iranian weapons have been supplied to Russia for use against Ukraine. "We're going in this merry-go-round where every bit of the conflict is linked to another," Stubb said. "The sooner we can end both, the better." Trump used his Sept. 22 U.N. General Assembly address to call for Iran's economic isolation and reiterate that Tehran should not obtain a nuclear weapon, while warning of further US military action if a peace agreement is not reached, according to Reuters. For Stubb, the proliferation of conflicts — from Ukraine and Iran to Gaza, Yemen and Sudan — is testing a diplomatic system already struggling to keep pace. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not a zero-sum game," he said. "We have to deal with a multiplicity of conflicts right now, unfortunately." And for Trump, he added, that means "working around the clock."
